source.title: Exploring Weak-to-Strong Generalization for CLIP-based Classification
source.authors: Jinhao Li; S. Erfani; Lei Feng; James Bailey; Feng Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It contains apparent inconsistencies in some table descriptions and reported averages; no values were inferred to resolve them.
record.tranche_reason: Tests weak-to-strong classification using CLIP-based vision-language models on image datasets, extending the setting beyond the original language tasks. It reports outcomes against weak-model and strong-ceiling references.
record.gate_note: Rows record reported weak-model, strong-ceiling, and selected weak-supervision method accuracies. CPL is the paper's proposed method, but its weak-supervision performance is included because it directly bears on whether the strong model beats its weak supervisor. The paper does not calculate PGR. Table 4 is described inconsistently as BLIP-based in the text while its table title and entries do not clearly establish the model; it is not included. Figure 2 reports accuracy curves without extractable values and is not separately rowed.
record.test_reason: The study runs the weak-to-strong protocol on image classification. A vision weak model (ResNet/ViT/CvT/ConvNeXt) is trained on ground truth, and its logits supervise CLIP through linear probing, prompt tuning or class-prototype learning (CPL). Results are reported against the weak model and a ground-truth strong ceiling on DomainNet, a weak-supervisor sweep and a CLIP-backbone sweep. These bear directly on V1, V2, V3 and V6. PGR is not computed but can be derived from the tabled accuracies.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that weak-to-strong generalization is feasible for CLIP-based classification, and that CPL beats LP/prompt-tuning baselines, including AuxConf and AdaptConf, by 3.67 points on DomainNet average. They add that gains are strongest when pretraining is limited. They acknowledge the simulations may not transfer to real superalignment. They also note that LP and prompt tuning overfit to the weak labels, landing near weak performance.
record.recipe_differences: Applies weak-model supervision to CLIP image classification and learns class prototypes, rather than the original language-model fine-tuning experiments and PGR calculation. It compares linear probing, prompt tuning, and confidence-loss variants as well.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary across DomainNet visual domains and weak-supervisor architectures. The paper reports that Quickdraw is especially challenging for CLIP. It also compares ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 CLIP variants on Clipart.
record.problems: The evidence is simulation-based and limited to classification; the authors say it may not transfer to the real-world problem. The paper reports five random seeds but gives no uncertainty estimates for the tabulated accuracies. PGR is not calculated. The reported tables/text contain inconsistencies, including the Sketch entry and the description of Table 4.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted the DomainNet average rows, KD+LP and KD+TP rows from Table 1, Table 3's non-CPL weak-to-strong methods and its stated average, Table 5's non-CPL methods, Table 6 OfficeHome results, Table 7 tuning comparison, and numeric extraction from Figure 2. Table 4 was not extracted because the text calls it BLIP-based while its displayed table content does not clearly establish the relevant model or setting.

untested.parts: Language-model tasks; PGR is not computed by the authors.
Ensembling weak supervisors; PGR-based comparison; uncertainty across the five seeds is not reported.
Chess, reward modelling, representational predictors of PGR; systematic scaling of the strong model beyond two CLIP backbones.
Vision tasks other than classification; non-CLIP strong models (Table 4's BLIP claim is unclear).

missing.what: Table 5 baselines on Clipart. Every method beats weak (ViT-B/16 weak 57.45: CE+LP 66.23, AuxConf+LP 69.45, AdaptConf+TP 73.78), so naive fine-tuning succeeds here, unlike DomainNet Table 1.
OfficeHome results. All methods beat weak, e.g. Art weak 54.78, CE+LP 62.10, CPL 70.45, ceiling 79.10. The weak average is missing from the table.
KD+LP/KD+TP and AuxConf+TP rows. KD+LP is the best baseline on Quickdraw (48.15). AuxConf+TP falls below CE+TP on Infograph (20.97 vs 29.25) and Quickdraw (43.60 vs 44.82).
Table 4 DomainNet results, described as BLIP-based, with a different weak model and ceiling (e.g. Clipart weak 60.23, CPL 72.45, ceiling 75.12). The pattern matches Table 1.
Table 3 non-CPL methods. All beat weak for ResNets and Cvt-13; for ConvNeXt (weak 69.47), CE+TP reaches only 67.71.
Prototype tuning versus text-encoder tuning: 74.42 vs 70.34 average.

record.verdict_notes: The record's Table 1 extraction is shifted by one column: Avg is the last column, not the first. This is verified by row averages (CE+LP mean 57.66) and by the Δ row. All Table 1 values, states and labels have been re-derived above; the claimed 'Sketch inconsistency' does not exist. Weak-model architecture for Table 1 is unstated (ResNet/ViT per implementation details). Table 3 labels the method 'CPL (BLIP)', and the strong model there is unclear. The strong ceiling is the best of LP/TP/CPL trained on ground truth. Five seeds were used, but no variance is reported.

versions.untested_parts: PGR itself is not calculated. The study tests CLIP-based classification in simulated image tasks, not language-model alignment or broader alignment behavior.
Reports selected comparisons among loss/tuning strategies but does not report PGR or a direct PGR comparison against every naive-fine-tuning configuration.
Tests DomainNet domains, several weak-model architectures on Clipart, and two CLIP variants on Clipart. It does not test chess, reward modelling, or representational predictors.
Supervisor-checking failures, distribution shift, and correlated weak/strong errors are not tested.
No theoretical conditions or proof that a student must beat its supervisor.
Tests vision-language image classification only; it does not test other modalities or general multimodal generation.
